title: Controlling red mite in a poultry house
subtitle: How to find, treat, and prevent the most damaging poultry parasite in UK flocks.
excerpt: Red mite live in the structure of the poultry house during the day and feed on birds at night. Heavy infestations cause anaemia, poor lay rates, and bird deaths. They are not visible on birds in daytime but their hiding places are easy to find with a torch. Here is how to check for them, treat the house, and reduce the likelihood of reinfestation.
sourceNotes: AHDB Poultry, red mite management guidance (2023). National Office of Animal Health, red mite treatment options. RSPCA welfare guidance on poultry ectoparasites.

glossaryTerms.definition: A blood-feeding ectoparasite that lives in cracks and joints of poultry housing. Feeds on birds at night, leaving birds anaemic. Appears red-brown after feeding; grey-white when unfed. Active above 5°C, most prolific in warm weather.

content.text: infestation often goes unnoticed until it is severe. The mites feed at night and return to cracks and joints in the structure by morning. The first signs are usually: pale combs in laying hens, a drop in egg production, restlessness at roosting time, or a faint grey dust in the joints of perches and nest boxes when you run your finger along them.
Check the house after dark with a torch. Red mites appear as tiny moving red or grey-white dots in joints, under perch ends, and at the edges of nest box lids.
During the day, check perch ends and nest box joints. A white piece of paper drawn along a joint will show red-staining if mites have been feeding recently.
Examine under any corrugated cardboard or straw left in the house. Mites use these as daytime refuges.
Move birds out during treatment. Strip all bedding and litter from the house and dispose of it well away from the poultry area.
Pressure wash the entire interior, paying particular attention to joints, cracks, and perch sockets. Allow to dry completely.

Apply a licensed treatment product. Options for small flocks licensed in the UK include Exzolt (in water or feed), diatom powders worked into cracks, and barrier products applied to joints. Follow the product label for repeat application timing.
Add fresh, dry bedding and return birds once the house is dry.
Repeat the treatment in 7 to 14 days to catch the next generation of hatching mites. One application rarely clears an established infestation.
Smooth-sided houses (plastic or powder-coated metal) harbour fewer mites than rough timber. Where timber is used, paint it with a sealant to reduce crevices.
Rotate perches and nest box inserts. Replacing them annually reduces the carryover population.
Wild birds carry mites. Net any roof openings that wild birds might enter through.
Check any second-hand equipment or new birds before introducing them to the flock.
